Egypt is seeking closer ties with Libya’s western government after years of backing its eastern rival. Talks in Tripoli covered energy projects and Egypt’s objections to Libya’s maritime deal with Turkey.

Egypt reopened its historic embassy building in the Libyan capital, Tripoli, on Saturday during a visit by Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty for talks on trade, energy and a disputed maritime boundary.

Libya’s acting foreign minister, Taher al-Baour, joined Abdelatty at the ceremony. Egypt closed the building in January 2014 after gunmen kidnapped five embassy staff. Its diplomatic mission resumed work in Tripoli in May 2021.

Cairo has long backed Khalifa Haftar, the military commander whose forces dominate eastern Libya, where a rival government is based. In Tripoli, Abdelatty met Abdulhamid Dbeibah, the prime minister of Libya’s internationally recognised Government of National Unity.

The two discussed ways to make trade easier. Dbeibah praised the role Egyptian companies and workers have played in rebuilding Libya, according to Egypt’s foreign ministry.

Abdelatty also met Libya’s acting oil minister at the reopened embassy. He called for faster progress on gas pipelines between the two countries and on plans to refine Libyan crude in Egypt for export. The Libyan minister said he would travel to Cairo for further talks, Libya’s state news agency reported on Sunday.

Why the maritime deal is disputed

In his talks with Dbeibah, Abdelatty raised Egypt’s objections to a 2019 agreement between Turkey and Libya’s then government in Tripoli. He said Egypt’s concerns should be taken into account when maritime boundaries are drawn, according to his ministry. Dbeibah told Egyptian broadcaster Al-Qahera News that officials from both countries would discuss the maps and their respective claims at their next meeting.

The agreement draws a boundary between Turkish and Libyan maritime zones in the eastern Mediterranean, where several countries claim rights to explore for oil and gas. Greece says the boundary ignores the rights of Greek islands, including Crete, which lies between the Turkish and Libyan coasts. Egypt and Cyprus also oppose the deal.

Libya’s eastern-based parliament ratified the agreement on 20 October after opposing it for years. The EU said the next day that the deal infringed on other countries’ rights and could have no legal effect on them. Turkish Foreign Minister Hakan Fidan defended it as “an entirely legitimate agreement, both from a legal and a political perspective”.

Italian company Eni is operating the Taiba concession in partnership with Australian company Woodside, while Egyptian firm Petrobel carried out the drilling work on behalf of the partners.

At this year's luxury watch awards, 84 timepieces and clocks were in competition across 14 categories, including sports, calendar and astronomy, jewellery and mechanical exception.

The Grand Prix d’Horlogerie de Genève (GPHG) awards returned for the 26th edition this year, showcasing the crème de la crème of luxury watchmaking at a glittering ceremony on 7 November.

The top honour, known as the ‘Aiguille d'Or’ Grand Prix, was open to any watch across all categories. Last year, it was won by Breguet's Classique Souscription 2025 - a watch which only has one hand. This year, it was awarded to an independent Swiss-Kosovan watchmaker making waves in horology.

“Aiguille d’Or” Grand Prix best-in-show award

The most distinguished award at the GPHG, the Aiguille d’Or, went to Geneva-based independent watchmaker Rexhep Rexhepi's Chronograph Flyback.

Sleek and harmonious, the proportions of this watch required "a complete rethinking of the movement’s architecture". The storm blue Grand Feu enamel dial draws inspiration from vintage pocket-watch chronographs.

The event once again highlighted the time-honoured mastery of the industry, as 84 watches and clocks vied for awards in 14 categories, including sports, calendar and astronomy, jewellery and mechanical exception.

In a first, the organisers scrapped the usual gender-based (Men’s and Ladies’) categories and replaced them with new technical categories: Essential Watch and Complication Watch.

The nominees this year included a Moscow workshop taking on the Swiss giants, a wearable solar system, and a 10-kilo clock that winds your watch while you sleep.

The winners were decided by a jury of experts including watch collectors, watchmakers, journalists and auctioneers.

Winners of the GPHG watchmaking awards

Here is the full list of winners of the night’s dazzling awards ceremony:

Time Only: Watches displaying only analogue time indications (hours, minutes, seconds) by means of two or three hands on a solid dial, devoid of any other type of indication, complications or gemsetting. One-of-a-kind models are not eligible for this category.

WINNER 2026: Chopard's L.U.C 1860 Chronometer

This watch was created as a continuation model of the original, iconic L.U.C 1860 to honour the 30th anniversary of Chopard Manufacture in Fleurier.

Essential: Watches displaying one or several of the following indications: hours, minutes, seconds, date (day of the month), power-reserve indicator, classic moon phases, day/night indicator. They may feature a digital or retrograde display and they may not fall within the respective definitions of the Time Only, Complication and Gemset categories. In Israel, a candidate tasked with forming a new government has 28 days to carry out the job. The president is able to extend this by a maximum of 14 days before giving the mandate to someone else.

Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of Israel's centrist Yashar party, is to be tasked with forming a new government after legislative elections last month produced no clear winner.

"President Isaac Herzog has decided to task Gadi Eisenkot, chairman of the ‘Yashar’ party, with forming a government," a statement from the president's office released on Saturday evening said.

The decision came after Herzog held talks with political figures over the last few days, including Eisenkot and main rival Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

Following the consultations, factions totalling 67 members of the Knesset (Israel's parliament) backed Eisenkot, while 46 supported Netanyahu, the statement said.

"The president has invited Gadi Eisenkot to the president’s residence for the ceremony to confer the mandate, which will take place tomorrow," it added.

A candidate tasked with forming a government has 28 days to carry out the job. The president is able to extend this by a maximum of 14 days if necessary.

Should that fail, the president can give a second leader the chance to form a government, this time with a maximum deadline of 28 days. If this second round were also to fail, then the Knesset can request a third candidate be given a go. They would have 14 days to complete the task.

If all attempts fail, another election is called.

Eisenkot, a former military chief, has vowed to "do everything" to form a new government.

Both Eisenkot and Netanyahu's blocs fell well short of a majority in the 120-seat Knesset in the recent elections.

Netanyahu's camp finished on 53 seats, while the opposition, led by the Yashar party, ended on 48.

Netanyahu's right-wing Likud party remained the largest party, with 27 seats, while the Arab parties secured a record 19 seats between them.

It comes after Netanyahu called on Saturday for the formation of a national unity government.

Six people were killed and 16 were injured after a shooting in Krakow's Main Market Square on Saturday afternoon, in what Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called an act of "terrorism."

Here's what we know about the attack.

The shooting took place at around 3 p.m. after a masked man in military clothing drove a car onto the popular tourist square and opened fire as people fled and sought shelter in nearby buildings.

After an exchange of fire with police, the suspect - a 24-year-old Polish citizen - was wounded, detained and taken to hospital, while his vehicle was checked for explosives.

Residents of nearby buildings were evacuated as the operation took place. The Main Market Square and adjoining streets were also closed.

The suspect

The suspect is said to be a resident of Ostrowiec Świętokrzyski in southeastern Poland.

He had no previous convictions and was not on police records. He held a firearms licence and likely fired shots from one of the weapons covered by that licence, per police.

Interior Minister Marcin Kierwiński said the gunman appeared to hold "very radical views" and was "fascinated by far-right ideologies."

Deputy Prime Minister and Defence Minister Władysław Kosiniak-Kamysz has denied reports that the suspect was a soldier in the Polish armed forces, saying he "has never had anything to do with the military."

Victims

Six people were killed in the shooting in Krakow, and a total of 16 people were injured, including two police officers and the suspect. One of the officers is in a serious condition.

Among those killed in the attack were four women and two men. One has been identified as a British citizen.

A Portuguese national and a Russian national are also reported to have been injured in the attack.

On Saturday evening, authorities announced that a further three bodies - two women and a man - had been discovered at the suspect's home. Tusk said there was "much to suggest that they are members of the (suspect's) immediate family."

Police later confirmed that the bodies of the perpetrator's 53-year-old father, 52-year-old mother and 20-year-old sister had been found at the home. The victims reportedly had gunshot wounds.

The interior minister also gave details about the injured officers. One officer was shot. The condition of the other is described as extremely serious, with the man having suffered three gunshot wounds.

"The police officers acted heroically today. They fulfilled their duty to the public and their country in an exemplary manner. One of them is fighting for his life. Another has been injured. I appeal to everyone to show respect for their sacrifice. To show respect for those in uniform," Kierwiński wrote on X.

Tusk named the officers who detained the suspect as senior constable Jakub Kulik and senior constable Artur Morański, calling them "true heroes."

"Their condition is serious, but they are receiving excellent care. The whole of Poland is keeping its fingers crossed for you," he said.

Weapons

According to police information, the suspect carried a semi-automatic gun similar in design to an AR-15 rifle. Photos from the scene also show an optical sight. The man also had a pistol.

Police secured a large number of other weapons and ammunition in his car.

National mourning declared

A two-day period of national mourning began at midnight on Sunday, with national flags flown at half-mast.

Websites are displaying black ribbons next to their logos and switching to subdued colours, while radio and television stations are altering their schedules. Entertainment events have also been cancelled.

The Norwegian capital is hosting the fifth edition of Fjord Oslo, an international festival showcasing outdoor light art. This year's edition brings together artists from several countries to explore the meaning of peace through installations across the city.

Oslo is lighting up with messages of peace as the Norwegian capital hosts the fifth edition of Fjord Oslo, an international festival of outdoor light art.

Taking place across the city, the festival brings together artists from different countries, with installations illuminating buildings, public spaces and the Nobel Peace Center.

This year's edition explores what peace means through art and shared experiences. It is part of IMAGINE PEACE, a European Union-funded cultural project.

The festival explores peace on a wider scale, looking at themes such as war, resilience, freedom and coexistence.

Organiser and light artist Anastasia Isachsen says holding the event in Oslo, home of the Nobel Peace Prize, gives the project particular significance. "Hopefully we send a strong message by dedicating our festival to the topic of peace. And again, it is about imagining what peace is on many different levels. It's also about global peace, international peace. But it's also on the personal level, what peace is for you as a person."

Croatian artist Marko Bolkovic says his team asked people in six countries to describe peace in just one word. "We asked a lot of people around the world, especially in this six countries that are part of the festival, what is peace for you to just say it in one word? And it was really interesting. Answers like father, friendship, mother, friends, things like that. Not always know war or other stuff."

Can art help change the way people think about peace?

Norwegian visitor Ulrich Lauridsen believes it can. "I definitely think that art can change things. Not like stop a war, but it can get more people to want to stop a war because life is too precious to have wars and conflicts and all that."

For Kenyan visitor Faith Imani, peace is above all about freedom. "I think it means freedom and for me, that's what it means, the freedom to leave, the freedom to exist, with each other, the freedom to be able to move within the world. So that is what peace means to me. The sense of freedom to just live and exist, coexist with everyone around."

Pack for tomorrow, not yesterday. A physicist says time travel to the past could be impossible.

A question many of us have posed in our minds is: where would you go if you had a time machine?

Would you crank the dial backwards like Marty McFly and risk sabotaging your own future? Before you start packing, a physicist has some news that may ruin a few Marvel movies: you may only be able to go one way, and it isn't backwards.

Hongsheng Zhang, a researcher at the University of Jinan in China, has shown that in a broad class of theoretical universes, travelling into your own past is impossible.

The whole argument rests on one fact. In relativity, the direction of light can never sit at right angles to an object’s direction through time.

Imagine spacetime sliced into layers that light itself can travel along. Anything moving slower or faster than light must cross these surfaces in the same direction, like climbing a staircase that never lets you step down.

If you can only ever go up, you can never arrive back on the step where you started.

The argument needs no exotic matter, no quantum effects and no assumptions about what fills the universe. "The whole content is bookkeeping about directions," Zhang told ScienceAlert.

The two loopholes

Physicists call journeys to the past "closed timelike curves": routes through spacetime that loop back to the very place and moment they began. Einstein's equations allow them in a handful of scenarios, such as near the core of a spinning black hole.

Crucially, Zhang's research - which is awaiting peer review - also reveals exactly how a time machine could achieve travelling back in time, and it claims there are only two ways.

The first is twist. Imagine light rays that, instead of travelling side by side, spiral around one another like the strands of a rope. When that happens, the neat surfaces of light can't form, so there is no one-dimensional staircase to keep you climbing.

This is what happens near the centre of a spinning black hole. Einstein’s theory says a spinning mass drags space and time around with it, an effect NASA’s Gravity Probe B satellite measured around Earth in 2011. Close to the black hole’s core the drag is so strong that moving “forward in time” is bent into a circle.

A traveller following that circle would see their clock ticking forward in time as normal, yet their journey would arrive back at the moment they set off. Physicist Brandon Carter showed in 1968 that such loops exist inside spinning black holes.

The second is the shape of the universe itself. The staircase might be perfectly built, but it could lead around the sides of a building, so the top step leads straight back to the bottom, like the impossible staircases in an Escher drawing. You would keep climbing and still end up where you began. Most of the time machines physicists have designed on paper, including those built from wormholes, rely on this trick.

The theorem has its limits, as Zhang acknowledges.

“What it does not do is tell us whether nature permits any of this. That remains open, and it is the question I would most like to see answered,” Zhang explained to ScienceAlert.

Destination: tomorrow

Trips to the future, by contrast, are already well established. Einstein showed that moving very fast, or sitting in strong gravity, slows your clock relative to everyone else's. Astronauts aboard the International Space Station return to Earth a few thousandths of a second younger than they would otherwise have been, according to the European Space Agency.

The work does not settle whether our own universe allows a journey to the past.

For now, though, anyone planning a trip may want to pack for tomorrow rather than yesterday... unless you have the Time Stone of course.

A prolonged period of cloudy and windless weather can throttle Europe's solar and wind generations, often causing the grid to rely on polluting back-up sources.

Europe risks entering its first ‘dunkelflaute’ of the year as cloudy weather dampens the continent’s solar boom and sends energy prices soaring.

Solar, which has been described as a “shining star” of the transition away from fossil fuels, is one of the quickest-to-install and cheapest forms of energy in the world. In the right conditions, it can cost as little as €0.024 to produce one unit of power via solar panels – far outperforming coal, gas and even wind.

It has already saved the EU €42.9 billion in avoided gas imports since the beginning of the war on Iran, which broke out on 28 February. It also helped stabilise the grid in the summer when back-to-back heatwaves triggered a spike in cooling-related electricity consumption.

But Europe’s prolonged period of cool, cloudy and windless weather pose a serious problem.

Can solar power perform in winter?

A dunkelflaute – German for ‘dark lull’ – is a term used to describe an extended period when wind and solar power generation are low or non-existent because there is not enough wind or sunlight.

It typically occurs from October through February in Northern Europe, exacerbated by short daylight hours, heavy cloud cover and fog. This coincides with increased energy consumption across the continent, due to chilly temperatures triggering demand for heating.

Multi-day dunkelflauten are rare, but such an occurrence pushes Europe’s energy grid to rely more heavily on expensive backup generation such as natural gas.

According to Bloomberg forecasts, German day-ahead power prices for Thursday 29 October were above €300 a megawatt-hour, about double the average in October, with hourly rates hitting above €500 for the evening peak.

‘It’s extremely disheartening’: Home solar output dips

On an individual scale, households with solar panels are also noticing a spike in their energy bills. One UK resident who has 12 solar panels installed on their roof with a combined capacity of 6.36 kW tells Euronews Earth that on Wednesday (4 November) the panels only produced 10.90 kWh of solar – leaving them to rely on the grid for an additional 27.40 kWh of energy required.

On Thursday (5 November), when their city was overcast for the entire day, the home generated just 2.40 kWh of solar, and imported 20.60 kWh.

This is despite having an 11.52 kWh home storage battery that is charged at night on an off-peak tariff to discharge in the day when electricity consumption increases.

Cloud is expected over the weekend and well into next week, meaning many Brits will be generating significantly less solar than they have during the summer.

“We’re hardly producing any power,” the resident, who wishes to remain anonymous, tells Euronews Earth.

“It’s extremely disheartening to see we’re importing so much energy when we have spent thousands on a solar system. However, we know that the panels will start to perform better when the clouds clear.”

Hydro steps in for solar’s dips

Of course, it is no surprise that solar produces most of its electricity in the summer months. In the EU, solar’s share of electricity generation hit 25.4 per cent in June – but in October this dropped to just 13.2 per cent.

Of course, solar relies on daylight opposed to heat - meaning homeowners with rooftop panels will still produce power even on cold days.

According to green energy supplier Good Energy, home solar systems in the UK can still generate around 25-35 per cent of their annual output in winter, which it says "provides a nice cushion for winter bills".

A dip in solar production also tends to coincide with increased generation of hydropower – which started to rise in the EU last year from October.

Solar is also able to help offset some of the electricity spikes caused by heatwaves, following a sudden need for space cooling, such as air conditioning and fans.

According to energy think tank Ember, during the late-June heatwave this summer, daily electricity demand rose by up to 28 per cent in Italy, 23 per cent in Hungary, 14 per cent in France and 13 per cent in Spain compared with pre-heatwave days.

It says that as heatwave-driven demand increased, solar was the only major power source to perform “better than usual”. Compared with other days in June and July, average daily solar generation during the heatwaves was 17 per cent higher in France and Hungary, five per cent higher in Spain and the same in Italy.

A typical UK home with rooftop solar generated enough electricity to power an A/C unit for five hours per day during the hot spell, a separate Ember analysis found.

At the same time, water-intensive forms of energy such as coal, hydropower and nuclear struggle during heatwaves – as scorching temperatures and lack of rainfall increase cause prolonged periods of drought.

In August, Poland was forced to reduce output on its coal-fired power plants, which require massive amounts of water for cooling, following critically low water levels in the Vistula River.

The move temporarily removed 1.3 GW from Poland’s power system, enough to power more than one million average households. This is around two per cent of the country’s current energy capacity.

From taking your shoes off indoors to being on time, a new survey reveals the social etiquette rules that travellers should know before heading to Europe.

A kiss on the cheek, turning up early or leaving food on your plate... little gestures can mean very different things across Europe.

Now, new research has revealed the etiquette rules travellers should know before heading to Europe, from greeting strangers to getting dinner right.

Preply, an online language learning and tutoring marketplace, looked at public data sources and surveyed 1,600 people living in 27 countries about European etiquette, and the results challenged some assumptions we’ve all probably been guilty of making.

While it might seem like etiquette isn’t a huge deal, it’s actually an important thing to consider when travelling to a country, where you’ll want to be kind, understanding and respectful of the people you meet.

It seems as though more people are understanding the necessity of the practice – and the proof is in the data.

As of September 2026, the #etiquette hashtag had reached some 4.4 billion views on TikTok, while searches for “how to have good etiquette” have risen by a staggering 373% in the past year alone.

When travelling in Europe, though, etiquette can change as quickly as the borders do, so it’s wise to be aware in order not to put a foot wrong. Here’s what the findings showed.

How to greet someone appropriately

You might associate Europeans with cheek kissing as a greeting, but it’s actually far less common than you might expect.

In 23 of 27 countries, the majority of people surveyed would actually wait for the other person to initiate two cheek kisses.

Across Europe, that figure is 85% and in Denmark, Estonia, Sweden, and Slovenia, respondents said they would reject the gesture outright.

Shoes on or off?

While not every country is as strict as Sweden – which saw 100% of respondents say it’s a must – taking off your shoes is common practice across the continent.

In 24 out of the 27 countries, most people said they would take their shoes off when visiting someone’s home.

Many countries in the north of Europe said indoor shoe removal was a must, and it was just Spain, Italy, and Portugal that disagreed, saying they preferred to keep their shoes on inside the home. That’s possibly down to warmer climates, which means houses have fewer carpets to protect.

Interestingly, there was an age divide, too.

Most respondents aged between 18 and 34 said they always took their shoes off, while those aged 35 to 54 preferred to wait until asked by the host.

To bring a gift or not to bring a gift?

Everyone likes to receive a gift from a visitor, but some like it more than others.

More than half of the survey respondents considered bringing a gift to be standard practice, while a third said they reserve gift-giving for special occasions.

Only Finland saw the majority say they’d never bring a host a gift.

The study found that respondents from 17 out of the 27 countries said they’d likely bring a bottle of wine or a bouquet of flowers when visiting a friend, although nine of that number – including Austria, the UK and Spain – said they’d reserve the gesture for a special occasion.

Make sure to finish your food

While opinions differ on most etiquette topics across Europe, finishing food was considered respectful across all 27 countries.

Seen as a universal marker of respect for the host’s effort, 82% of men said they always finished meals, compared to 75% of women.

Some female respondents said they were more likely to deliberately leave a little left, possibly out of a sense of politeness.

Punctuality is a divisive issue

Online searches for the term “is it better to be on time, early or late?” were, according to Preply, up 66% globally over the past year, and the data reveals a somewhat complicated answer.

In 23 out of 27 countries, respondents favoured arriving on time, with Greece particularly keen on punctuality, while 35% of men said they prefer to arrive early, a higher figure than female respondents who aim to arrive on time.

Respondents in Czechia, Germany, Poland, and France said they preferred to arrive early at a destination.

The survey found that single people were twice as likely to arrive late, and those with children found it particularly hard to keep to a rigid schedule.
